newsitem.title: USA: U.S. wholesale inventories rose in March.
newsitem.headline: U.S. wholesale inventories rose in March.

text.p: Wholesalers were left with higher inventories in March as sales took their largest drop since last summer, the Commerce Department said on Wednesday.
Wholesale sales fell 0.9 percent in March -- the steepest decline since last August -- to a seasonally adjusted $209.88 billion after a 2.1 percent gain in February, the department said.
Sales were especially slow for costly and long-lasting durable goods, which fell 1.7 percent in March. The biggest drops were in furniture, lumber, metals and machinery sales, the department said.
Sales of quickly used nondurables slipped a scant 0.1 percent in March as paper, apparel, farm product, petroleum and chemical sales declined, while drug, grocery and alcohol sales rose, it said.

Total wholesale inventories rose 0.7 percent in March to a seasonally adjusted $259.89 billion. The largest build-ups were in automobiles, electrical equipment and machinery, while stocks of furniture, professional equipment and hardware declined, it said.

With sales off and inventories up, wholesalers' inventory- to-sales ratio -- a measure of how long it would take to deplete existing stocks at the current sales pace -- recovered slighty to 1.24 months' worth in March from an extremely low 1.22 months' worth in February, the department said.
Low inventory levels relative to sales suggest that manufacturers have room to boost production to build stocks.
The department said it changed the sample base and sample design it uses for its monthly survey of wholesalers, which it said should provide more accurate data and reduce revisions.
